newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS - Thai PM says worst over, recovery imminent.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Thai PM says worst over, recovery imminent.

text.p: Thailand has weathered the worst of its recent economic downturn, and while recovery is imminent people must be patient, Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh said on Monday.
Chavalit said he was confident in his government's ability to bring the economy back to life, and shrugged off the fact that the Stock Exchange of Thailand had plunged to eight-year lows last week.

"Everything is still all right...Be patient," Chavalit said in an interview with a small group of foreign journalists. "We have to try to stop the downturn. But I think it's come to its lowest point already. People will be happy now, everything will be coming up."
The Stock Exchange of Thailand tumbled to new eight-year low last week amid a slowing economy and a lack of confidence in the government's ability to jump-start it.

The drop was also due to rumours of political discord in the cabinet over unelected Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan's ability to handle the crisis. Chavalit denied the talk of dissent and has said Amnuay would not step down.
Investors were also unloading stocks due to currency uncertainty and questions over whether Thai authorities would be forced to devalue the baht.
Chavalit said his government was united and predicted things should start looking better by July. He also said the government was steadfast in its pledge to defend the baht from any further attacks.
He said the government would not devalue the baht, and said the economy remained the key focus of his six-month old administration.

Chavalit said the government would step in if necessary to stop speculators if they attacked the currency like last week when they aggressively sold baht for dollars amid rumours of a possible baht devaluation.
"They can try again. We'll fight with all we have. This is the last line of defence," Chavalit said.
The Bank of Thailand teamed up with other regional central banks last week to intervene in foreign exchange markets to defend the baht from a fierce attack by offshore speculators.
Chavalit also said the government planned to announce new measures later this week to boost the ailing property sector which has been hard hit by the sluggish economy and a liquidity crunch.
He said the new measures, in addition to others announced at the weekend by Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan, should bring confidence and liquidity back to the market.
On Saturday, Amnuay said commercial banks would pool 50 billion baht ($1.92 billion) for a rescue fund to help shore up the battered market which has lost more than 32 percent this year.
The market rebounded on Monday and finished up 2.84 percent, boosted in part by the rescue fund and on expectations of stronger exports, brokers said.
The bourse took its latest hammering last week when investors dumped more shares in response to the heavy speculation on the baht amid rumours of a devaluation.
Stocks have also been hurt by expectations that the economy will slow to about five to six percent this year -- a sharp drop from the average nine percent growth Thailand posted over the past decade.
But Chavalit said the current account deficit was narrowing, inflation was falling and short-term debt was declining.
"Our economic infrastructure is very good," he said. ($1 = 26 baht)
